architecture.fell_back_and_why: All six research sub-agents returned; nothing was dropped for non-return. Dispatched in two waves within the four-in-flight cap (wave 1: fieldops-api, pulumi-platform, settlement-worker, atlas-rag; wave 2: atlas-android, warehouse-dbt), each wave collected before the next was sent. Deviations from the reference pipeline, all forced by the read-only and offline constraints: (a) state_root was placed OUTSIDE the target at scratchpad/mantis-run-1/ per the meta-agent's colocated-state rule, and the run was MODE-OFF (no --sync, no snapshot pinned, discovery_commit omitted); (b) Stage 1 summarize normally writes mantis-summary.md into each target directory -- redirected to workspace/kb/ and workspace/summaries/ because the target is read-only; (c) Stage 11 patch was not run at all, since it mutates the target; (d) Stage 5's Wave-1 lightweight triage was collapsed into Wave-2 deep audits because the corpus is 60 files / 4,477 lines, small enough that triage would have discarded nothing; (e) the supervisor also read the full corpus itself so that Stage 7 review and Stage 8 critic were grounded in the source rather than in the researchers' prose, as mantis-review requires ('explicitly ignore the original finder's prose reasoning'); (f) Stage 13 reflect received an EXPLICIT EMPTY transcript list -- this harness exposes no per-subagent transcript path -- and the missing-transcript insight is recorded here rather than silently emitting zero learnings.
architecture.notes_on_delegation: The six researchers produced 44 raw findings. Stage 6 found no cross-agent duplicates (each covered one component) and merged 3 within-component pairs. Stage 7 rejected 2 researcher findings outright and downgraded 1 from medium to low. 7 findings in this report were added by the supervisor's own sweep or by Stage 10 chaining.

stages_skipped: mantis-history (Stage 0) -- the target tree contains no .git/.hg/.repo, so there is no VCS history to mine and workspace/historical_learnings.jsonl is empty. Nothing was inferred from commit history.

mantis-structural-index (Stage 0.5) -- no prebuilt SCIP/Kythe index, no ctags and no query_structural_index.py helper in this environment. The skill declares the index HINT-only with grep as the documented fallback, so discovery degraded to exhaustive grep over a 60-file corpus with no loss of membership.

mantis-reproduce (Stage 9) -- ran only at tier 1 (unit micro-harness) and could not reach tier 2 or tier 3. Measured, not assumed: docker, pulumi, dbt, redis-server, psql and gradle are all absent, and no component's dependencies are installed (python3 -c 'import pydantic' and 'import jsonschema' both fail), so no sandboxed service could be stood up offline. Two tier-1 harnesses DID run, both against source extracted from the target rather than retyped: (1) the real body of scrubNotes (fieldops-api/src/lib/policy.ts:57-63) executed under node -- '', '' all pass through unchanged, which is what makes the stored-XSS finding confirmed rather than argued; (2) the Reference pattern extracted from settlement-worker/settlement/schemas.py:16 tested against SQL payloads -- every quote-bearing and over-length value rejected, which is what demoted the ledger.py:81 SQL injection to low/probable instead of reporting it as a high. Everything else in this report is static-confirmed only.
mantis-patch (Stage 11) -- deliberately not run. It writes fixes into the target and the engagement is read-only. No file under the target was modified; recommendations are given as text only.

triage_rule_map.convention: FP-01..FP-13 are the 13 negative constraints of mantis-review/SKILL.md Step 3, in its own order. 'answer' states whether the false-positive condition that rule describes HOLDS for the finding. HOLDS = the rule fires and would dismiss the finding (MANTIS outcome FAIL); DOES_NOT_HOLD = the finding survives that rule (MANTIS PASS); NOT_APPLICABLE and UNKNOWN carry their MANTIS meaning. Because every reported finding survived review, its triage entries are DOES_NOT_HOLD, NOT_APPLICABLE or UNKNOWN -- with one deliberate exception noted below. Entries in provenance.ruled_out carry the rule that HELD and killed the assertion. Rules not listed on a finding were evaluated and came out DOES_NOT_HOLD; only the load-bearing ones are written out, and FP-12 is stated on every finding because it is the anti-hallucination check.
triage_rule_map.recorded_rule_conflict: One finding (settlement-worker ledger.py:81) carries FP-03 = HOLDS and is still reported. That is a genuine conflict between rule 3 and rule 8, surfaced rather than hidden: rule 8 orders an intrinsic injection path to be marked VALID 'even if it is not currently called anywhere', while rule 3 would dismiss it for having no reproducible trigger. Rule 8 is the more specific rule and wins, and the conflict is why that finding is low/probable rather than a high-severity SQL injection.

provenance.calibration_note: mantis-calibrate caps a statically-confirmed finding below CRITICAL when no reproducer ran. Stage 9 reached tier 1 only, so nothing in this report is rated above 'high' -- which also happens to be the ceiling of the requested severity scale. 'confirmed' means the defect and its reachability are both established from source read at the cited lines (and, for two findings, measured); 'probable' means the defect is certain but a load-bearing reachability or impact question could not be settled from this snapshot, and each such finding says which question in its triage.

ruled_out.assertion: Remote code execution: the ?template= query parameter is compiled with new Function and executed.
ruled_out.killed_by: printQuery is declared .strict() at workorders.ts:168 and zValidator feeds the whole query map to zod, so an unknown `template` key fails validation and the handler never runs. The new Function call at :186 is unreachable from the query string.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the interpolated limit and offset in the list query.
ruled_out.killed_by: Both values are clamped to integers before interpolation at workorders.ts:50-51: Number.parseInt with a `|| 0` / `|| 50` fallback, then Math.max/Math.min. No non-numeric string can reach the SQL string.

ruled_out.assertion: Rate-limit key spoofing by supplying a forged X-Forwarded-For header.
ruled_out.killed_by: The code takes the LAST hop (hops[hops.length-1]) and AWS ALB appends the observed client address to the end of the header, so the entry read is the one the ALB wrote, not the attacker's. The cf-connecting-ip fallback at :17 is unreachable behind an ALB, which always sets XFF.

ruled_out.assertion: User enumeration through differential responses on the password-recovery endpoint.
ruled_out.killed_by: session.ts:120 returns {status:'sent'} unconditionally, outside the `if (principal)` block, so the response does not vary with existence.

ruled_out.assertion: Stored XSS by uploading an attachment with an attacker-chosen text/html content type.
ruled_out.killed_by: attachments.ts:103-104 sets content-disposition: attachment and x-content-type-options: nosniff, so the browser downloads rather than renders; the filename is escaped at :103 and stripped by SAFE_NAME at :50.

ruled_out.assertion: Arbitrary SQL execution through the run_sql tool.
ruled_out.killed_by: run_sql is absent from TOOL_SPECS (tools.py:64-89) and from TOOL_REGISTRY (tools.py:91-94); dispatch resolves names only through the registry (tools.py:99), and a corpus-wide grep finds no other call site. Not reachable.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection or tenancy override through the caller-supplied `filters` object.
ruled_out.killed_by: The WHERE clauses are literal strings and only `source_kind` is admitted (retriever.py:59-61); every value is bound (:72-75). tenant_id and collection are overwritten from the principal AFTER the filter copy (:56-57), and `vector`/`k` are overridden by explicit kwargs at :72.

ruled_out.assertion: Wildcard CORS allows a malicious site to read another user's answers.
ruled_out.killed_by: The service is bearer-only: cors_allow_credentials is False (settings.py:44), the middleware never emits Access-Control-Allow-Credentials (app.py:250-259), and _require_principal reads only the Authorization header (app.py:72). A browser cannot attach a victim's credential cross-origin, so `*` grants nothing a key holder does not already have.

ruled_out.assertion: Cross-tenant document write through POST /v1/documents.
ruled_out.killed_by: app.py:186 binds tenant_id=principal.tenant_id and DOCUMENT_SCHEMA (app.py:33-47, validated at :179) constrains the collection to an enum and the acl entries to a pattern the literal '*' cannot match.

ruled_out.assertion: The publicly readable legacy archive bucket exposes migrated export objects.
ruled_out.killed_by: createLegacyArchive is exported but has no call site anywhere in the corpus (grep returns only its own definition), so the bucket, its disabled public access block and its Principal:'*' policy are never created by either stack.

ruled_out.assertion: The production exports bucket is anonymously readable.
ruled_out.killed_by: Pulumi.prod.yaml:7 sets publicExports false, so the public access block at storage.ts:44-47 is fully on and the `if (args.publicExports)` branch at :50 never runs in prod. Only the staging stack is affected, and that is reported as its own finding.

ruled_out.assertion: The reports bucket is publicly exposed because its public access block leaves blockPublicPolicy and restrictPublicBuckets false.
ruled_out.killed_by: The only policy attached to that bucket names a specific role ARN (storage.ts:125), which S3 does not classify as a public policy, so the relaxed flags grant no anonymous access as configured.

ruled_out.assertion: The RDS primary is exposed by the 0.0.0.0/0 ingress rule on the shared DB security group.
ruled_out.killed_by: data.ts:47 sets publiclyAccessible:false on the primary and its subnet group uses privateSubnetIds whose route table has no default route (network.ts:38-41), so the open security group rule has no reachable path to it. Only the replica is exposed, and that is reported separately.

ruled_out.assertion: dropInvalidHeaderFields:false is what allows the x-fieldops-* spoofing.
ruled_out.killed_by: The flag only drops headers with RFC-invalid names; well-formed x-fieldops-* headers pass through whether it is true or false. Treating it as the weakness would misdirect the fix; the real defect is the absent mutual TLS, reported as its own finding.

ruled_out.assertion: The /ops/* listener rule exposes Prometheus and Alertmanager because it has no authenticate-oidc action.
ruled_out.killed_by: The WAF rule at edge.ts:161-188 blocks the /ops/ prefix for any source outside the corporate IpSet (edge.ts:145-149), and path variants that dodge the ALB pathPattern at :139 fall through to the fixed 404 default action at :84-89.

ruled_out.killed_by: Both are publishable client-side values, documented as such and identical across stacks (Pulumi.staging.yaml:18-20, Pulumi.prod.yaml:14; build.gradle.kts:20-23). A pk_test_ publishable key and a signature-restricted tile key carry no authority.

ruled_out.assertion: The subnet CIDR 10.1.x.x falls outside the VPC CIDR 10.0.0.0/16.
ruled_out.killed_by: Real defect, but a deploy-time correctness failure rather than a reachability or authorization exposure -- the stack fails to create the subnet rather than creating an exposed one.

Noted because the sink is genuinely unescaped at :79 while the title beside it is encoded at :78 -- it becomes live the moment a caller appears. ruled_out.killed_by: Its only caller compares the host first: AuthInterceptor.kt:19 returns early unless host == BuildConfig.API_HOST. The misleading signature is a maintenance hazard, not a reachable flaw.

ruled_out.killed_by: The check fails closed: Uri.getHost() does not lowercase, so a mixed-case host misses the set at :43 and falls through to goHome(). A bypass would require the check to fail open, and it does not.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the partner_id variable interpolated into the export model's WHERE clause.
ruled_out.killed_by: partner_extract.sql:16 applies modules.re.sub("[^a-z0-9-]", "", requested_partner | lower), leaving only [a-z0-9-]: no quote, semicolon, whitespace, backslash or comment character survives, and a fully stripped value yields partner_id = '' , which fails closed. The max_rows variable on line 58 is guarded by an `| int` filter.

ruled_out.assertion: The tenant isolation policy covers only SELECT, leaving INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE unrestricted across tenants.
ruled_out.killed_by: Postgres default-denies any command that has no matching policy once row level security is enabled, so write commands fail closed rather than escaping the policy. The scope/docstring mismatch is documentation drift and is noted inside the RLS finding rather than filed as an exposure.

ruled_out.assertion: An unset app.tenant_id session variable disables tenant filtering.
ruled_out.killed_by: current_setting('app.tenant_id', true) returns NULL when unset and `tenant_id = NULL` is never true, so an unconfigured session sees zero rows. Fails closed.

ruled_out.assertion: The project's apply_grants macro shadows dbt-core's built-in of the same name, so the +grants blocks are dead configuration and dbt's revoke-diff never runs.
ruled_out.killed_by: Could not be settled in this run and is therefore not asserted. dbt is not installed and the run is offline, and the collision's most likely observable outcome is a loud Jinja arity error -- dbt's materialisations call apply_grants with three arguments including should_revoke, while this macro declares one -- rather than a silent policy substitution. Recording it as an open question rather than a finding; the grants the macro DOES issue are reported on their own evidence.

ruled_out.assertion: grant_all_to_analysts hands ALL PRIVILEGES to analyst_role.
ruled_out.killed_by: No call site: a corpus-wide grep returns only the definition. Superseded per its own comment by the per-folder +grants blocks.

ruled_out.assertion: Warehouse connections are made without certificate validation.
ruled_out.killed_by: All three targets set sslmode: verify-full with a pinned CA bundle (profiles.yml:17-18, 29-30, 41-42). The strongest available setting is already in use.

ruled_out.assertion: Unbounded in-memory growth of the rate-limit and replay maps is a denial-of-service vector.
ruled_out.killed_by: Resource-exhaustion finding of exactly the class rule 7 excludes; neither module's stated purpose is DoS defence, and no eviction contract is claimed. The same disposition applies to the unbounded bucket map at fieldops-api/src/middleware/rateLimit.ts:8.

ruled_out.assertion: Ingest and credential routes on the RAG service are not rate limited.
ruled_out.killed_by: limits.allow is applied only to /v1/query. Treated as the missing-limit class rule 7 excludes rather than a finding of its own; the substantive part -- that credential minting is reachable with the published demo key -- is reported as its own low-severity finding.

ruled_out.assertion: The /api/* listener rule is a security flaw because it carries no authenticate-oidc action.
ruled_out.killed_by: The API authenticates its own callers: requireAuth returns 401 when it cannot name the caller (fieldops-api/src/middleware/auth.ts:62-64). The genuine defect on this path is that the identity headers are forgeable, which is reported as its own finding.

ruled_out.assertion: The /healthz and /v1/health endpoints leak sensitive deployment detail.
ruled_out.killed_by: They return the environment name, a cache entry count and the configured model name. Missing-hygiene class; no principal, tenant or credential data.

findings.title: Unauthenticated identity spoofing: the API trusts x-fieldops-* headers in production and the load balancer never sets or strips them
findings.class: authentication bypass (CWE-290 spoofing of a trusted proxy identity)
findings.evidence: config.ts:28 sets `trustProxyIdentity: (env.NODE_ENV ?? 'development') === 'production'`, so the fallback is ON exactly where it matters. auth.ts:59-61: `if (!actor && config.trustProxyIdentity) { actor = fromProxyHeaders(c.req.raw.headers); }`. fromProxyHeaders (auth.ts:45-54) builds the whole principal out of request headers: `id = headers.get('x-fieldops-actor')`, `orgId = headers.get('x-fieldops-org')`, `role = headers.get('x-fieldops-role') as Role` (an unchecked cast, so 'admin' is accepted), `crewIds` split from `x-fieldops-crews`. The premise that makes this safe is stated at auth.ts:41-44 and edge.ts:32-35 -- the ALB terminates client certificates and puts the resolved principal on the request. The infrastructure does not do that: the HTTPS listener at edge.ts:78-90 declares sslPolicy and certificateArn and has no `mutualAuthentication` and no `trustStoreArn`, there is no aws.lb.TrustStore resource anywhere in pulumi-platform, and the /api/* rule at edge.ts:93-97 is a bare `forward` with no authenticate action. Nothing in the program strips x-fieldops-* from an inbound request. The ALB security group accepts 0.0.0.0/0 on 443 (network.ts:76).
findings.impact: Any internet client can assert an arbitrary actor id, an arbitrary orgId and role 'admin' with no credential, no certificate and no token, by sending three headers and no Authorization header. requireAuth returns 200 and every downstream authorization decision -- tenancy in workorders.ts:123/176, canWriteSite, visibleCrewFilter -- is made against attacker-chosen values. This is a complete pre-authentication cross-tenant takeover of the work-order API.
findings.recommendation: Fix the platform half and the application half together. Platform: configure `mutualAuthentication: { mode: 'verify', trustStoreArn: ... }` on the listener at edge.ts:78-90, and have the listener overwrite (not merely forward) the x-fieldops-* headers from the verified certificate. Application: until the listener provably sets them, delete the fromProxyHeaders path; a header is not a credential. If the path must stay, gate it on a shared secret header that the listener injects and that no client can forge, and stop casting `x-fieldops-role` straight to Role.

triage.reason: Ingress is the raw HTTP request; the tainted values are read at auth.ts:46,50,51,52 straight from headers an internet client controls. No trusted-origin argument survives, because the component that was supposed to author them (mTLS at the ALB) is not configured.

The claimed mitigation was checked and does not exist: the entire LoadBalancer (edge.ts:27-37) and Listener (edge.ts:78-90) declarations were read line by line and contain no mutualAuthentication, no trustStoreArn, and no header sanitisation.
Not a missing-header/hygiene item: this is the primary authentication decision returning success for an unauthenticated caller.
Trigger is three static headers on one request; deterministic, no timing or environmental fragility.
auth.ts:45,51,59, config.ts:28, edge.ts:35,78,93 all read and confirmed present at those lines.

scope.established_by: config.ts:28 enables the path for NODE_ENV=production; auth.ts:59-61 is the branch that consumes it; edge.ts:78-90 is the listener that was supposed to make it safe and does not.
scope.narrowed_by: Only reachable when NODE_ENV === 'production'; in development/staging trustProxyIdentity is false and fromProxyHeaders is never called. attachActor (auth.ts:74-78) does not use the proxy path at all.

findings.title: Stored XSS in the printable work-order sheet: title is never sanitised and notes survive the scrubber, both rendered unescaped
findings.class: stored cross-site scripting (CWE-79)
findings.evidence:
Two fields reach the same HTML response unescaped while their neighbours are escaped. workorders.ts:197 `
${wo.notes}
` -- raw, one line after escapeHtml is used on siteId and status at :194-195. workorders.ts:191 `
${render(wo)}
` -- render is the compiled DEFAULT_SHEET `

${wo.title}

` (:162,:186), so title is emitted raw at :191 and escaped at :192, the same value treated both ways in adjacent lines. title has no sanitiser at all on the write path (workorders.ts:101 passes body.title straight through; only notes get scrubNotes). notes are scrubbed, but the scrubber is tag-name-based: I executed the actual function body extracted from policy.ts:57-63 under node and measured its output -- '' -> unchanged; '' -> unchanged; only '' was removed. hono's secureHeaders() (index.ts:16) sets no Content-Security-Policy by default, so nothing downstream blocks execution. The response is served as text/html by c.html at :200.
findings.impact: Any actor who can create or patch a work order stores script that executes in the browser of every dispatcher, manager or admin who opens that order's print sheet, in the API's own origin, with the victim's session. Title needs 30 characters and is bounded only by max(200) at :27. Consequences: session-scoped actions as a higher-privileged role, and reading any org data the victim can reach.
findings.recommendation: Escape both sinks: `${escapeHtml(wo.notes)}` at :197 and escape the render output at :191 (or drop the new Function template machinery entirely and build the header with escapeHtml like the rest of the document). Treat scrubNotes as a display-time convenience, never as the control -- an allow-list sanitiser or contextual escaping is the control. Add a Content-Security-Policy to secureHeaders().

triage.reason: Ingress is the authenticated request body at workorders.ts:87 (createBody.title/notes) and :113 (patchBody); an attacker-controlled writer, persisted, then rendered to a different user.
The mitigation was tested rather than assumed: scrubNotes was executed on its own source and lets event-handler payloads through. The title path has no mitigation at all.
Not paranoia about a safe library: these are two raw interpolations sitting beside four correctly escaped ones in the same template.
Deterministic: one POST then one GET. The sanitiser bypass is measured, not argued.
workorders.ts:191,192,194,197 and policy.ts:57-63 read and confirmed.
code_paths carry the two sink lines and the sanitiser; the caller files are not included.

scope.established_by: The print handler at workorders.ts:170-201 renders the sheet; policy.ts:57-63 is the sanitiser that both vectors rely on.
scope.narrowed_by: Only the html format branch is affected -- `?format=json` returns at :181 before any HTML is built. Reached only by a caller inside the same org, because the row lookup at :175 pins org_id.

findings.title: Legacy /files mount is behind soft authentication, and the attachment handlers skip the tenancy check entirely when no actor is present
findings.class: broken access control / fail-open authorization (CWE-306)
findings.evidence: index.ts:28 puts `requireAuth` on `/api/v1/*` only. index.ts:35-36 mounts the SAME attachments router a second time under `config.legacyFilesMount` ('/files', config.ts:32) with `attachActor`, which by construction never rejects: auth.ts:74-78 sets the actor when a token parses and calls next() either way. Both read handlers then guard with `if (actor && actor.orgId !== row.orgId)` (attachments.ts:80 and :97) -- the check is skipped, not failed, when actor is undefined. The comment at attachments.ts:78-79 says the grant 'rides on the link itself', but no signature, expiry or token is parsed anywhere in the file. Attachment rows are fetched by id alone (attachments.ts:24-32).
findings.impact: An unauthenticated internet caller who holds or guesses an attachment id reads that attachment's metadata via GET /files/:id and its bytes via GET /files/:id/raw, with no session and across any tenant. The pre-signed-link design the comment describes is not implemented, so there is nothing to verify.
findings.recommendation: Put requireAuth on the legacy mount too, or if unauthenticated links are genuinely required, implement and verify the signature (HMAC over id plus expiry) before the row is returned. Change both guards from `if (actor && ...)` to a positive check that denies when no actor and no valid link grant is present.

triage.reason: Ingress is the unauthenticated HTTP request path parameter at attachments.ts:74/:93.
Not a hypothetical caller misusing a safe function: the mount is written this way in index.ts:35 and the fail-open guard is in the handler itself.
Not missing hygiene -- it is an authorization check that is bypassed rather than absent by design.

Reading a specific attachment requires knowing its id; ids are DB-assigned and not shown in the snapshot's schema, so id guessability could not be settled here. The missing check itself is unambiguous.
index.ts:35,36, config.ts:32, attachments.ts:80,97 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: index.ts:35-36 mounts the router without requireAuth; the two `if (actor && ...)` guards are what turn a missing actor into a pass.
scope.narrowed_by: The upload handler on the same mount is not exploitable: attachments.ts:62 dereferences actor.orgId and throws when the soft middleware left no actor.

findings.title: Work-order list cache is keyed on org, status and page but the response body depends on the caller's crew narrowing
findings.class: cache poisoning / horizontal privilege escalation (CWE-524)
findings.evidence: cache.ts:11-13 builds the key as `wo:list:${orgId}:${status}:${page}`. workorders.ts:53 uses exactly that key, then workorders.ts:60 computes `const crews = visibleCrewFilter(actor)` and workorders.ts:67-70 appends `and crew_id = any(...)` only when crews is non-null. policy.ts:47-50: techs get their own crewIds, dispatchers and managers get null (no narrowing). So two callers in the same org, same status tab, same page produce different row sets and share one cache slot. `limit` is likewise absent from the key while it changes the payload (workorders.ts:51,72). The entry lives listCacheTtlSeconds = 45s (config.ts:38).
findings.impact: A dispatcher or manager warms the slot with the whole org board; for the next 45 seconds any tech in that org hitting the same tab and page is served it from cache (x-cache: hit) and sees work orders for crews they are not on. The inverse also holds: a tech's narrowed page is served to a dispatcher, silently hiding work. The exposure stays inside one org because orgId is in the key.
findings.recommendation: Include everything the response depends on in the key: the crew filter (or the role) and the limit -- e.g. `wo:list:${orgId}:${status}:${page}:${limit}:${crews?.join(',') ?? 'all'}`. Better, cache per principal, or do not cache a row set whose membership is authorization-dependent.

triage.reason: Not a data-flow-to-sink finding: the defect is that an authorization-dependent result is stored under an authorization-independent key. No taint source is required.
Both callers are legitimate uses of the exported API; the key construction itself is the flaw.
Reproducible on demand: one dispatcher request then one tech request inside 45s, and the x-cache header at :56 reports the hit.
Not a resource-exhaustion claim.

findings.title: BOOTSTRAP_SQL grants ALL then revokes four verbs, leaving UPDATE on the append-only journal
findings.class: excessive database privilege (CWE-732)
findings.evidence: ledger.py:19-24 reads `GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA settlement TO settlement_app; REVOKE DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA settlement FROM settlement_app; REVOKE ALL ON settlement.journal FROM PUBLIC;`. GRANT ALL on a Postgres table confers SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER; the revoke lists four of the seven and omits UPDATE. The third statement targets PUBLIC, a distinct pseudo-role, and does not affect privileges granted directly to settlement_app. The comment two lines above (ledger.py:16-18) states the intended invariant: 'the destructive verbs are taken back so an application bug cannot erase audit history'. The same role is re-granted insert and update on the warehouse relations every dbt run by warehouse-dbt/macros/apply_grants.sql:25, so a manual revoke would not stick there either.

findings.recommendation: Stop granting ALL and subtracting: grant the two verbs the writer needs explicitly (`GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON settlement.journal TO settlement_app`). If the broad grant must stay, add UPDATE to the revoke list at ledger.py:21. Enforce append-only in the database with a rule or trigger owned by a different role.

Both candidate mitigations were checked and rejected: the REVOKE at :21-22 does not list UPDATE, and the REVOKE ... FROM PUBLIC at :23 does not reach a direct grant to settlement_app.
Not a hygiene item: the comment declares an invariant that the SQL does not deliver.

findings.title: Hostless https intent-filter lets any app or web page hand the deep-link router an arbitrary URL to load in the WebView
findings.class: improper URI handling on an exported component (CWE-940)
findings.evidence: AndroidManifest.xml:47-52 declares a BROWSABLE VIEW filter with `<data android:scheme="https" android:pathPrefix="/r/" />` and no android:host. With no host element the filter matches any authority, and autoVerify has nothing to verify against, so App Links verification cannot bind it to a domain. The activity is android:exported="true" (AndroidManifest.xml:33). DeepLinkRouter.kt:35 routes the https scheme to routeWeb, and routeWeb takes the destination straight from the incoming URI: `val target = uri.getQueryParameter("target") ?: "${BuildConfig.API_BASE}${uri.path}"` (DeepLinkRouter.kt:62), then `startActivity(ReportWebViewActivity.intentFor(this, target))` (:63). Nothing validates the scheme, host or prefix of target. The contrast is deliberate in the same file: the atlas:// branch does check, restricting the host to ALLOWED_HOSTS at DeepLinkRouter.kt:43, and openOrder/openReport build their URLs from BuildConfig.API_BASE (:72, :90). The comment at :56-59 asserts the https branch is safe because 'the intent filter is verified against our domain association file' -- the manifest does not implement that.

findings.recommendation: Add android:host with the real report domain to the filter at AndroidManifest.xml:51 so autoVerify can bind it. In routeWeb, stop honouring the caller's `target` parameter, or accept it only after parsing it and requiring scheme https and host == BuildConfig.API_HOST. Treat every value arriving on an exported component as untrusted, the way the atlas:// branch already does.

The claimed mitigation was checked against the manifest and does not exist: the filter has no host, so neither pathPrefix scoping nor autoVerify constrains the origin.
Production activity declared in the shipping manifest.
Deterministic: one intent. Requires only that the user is signed in (DeepLinkRouter.kt:28).

scope.narrowed_by: Only the https branch is affected. The atlas:// branch is constrained by ALLOWED_HOSTS at DeepLinkRouter.kt:43, and the router returns early unless SessionStore.isSignedIn() (:28).

findings.title: The Atlas JavaScript bridge returns the raw session bearer to whatever page the WebView happens to load
findings.class: sensitive data exposed to untrusted web content (CWE-749)
findings.evidence: ReportWebViewActivity.kt:44 enables JavaScript, :57 registers the bridge unconditionally -- `web.addJavascriptInterface(ReportBridge(), "Atlas")` -- and only afterwards, at :59-62, does it read the URL from the intent and call loadUrl. The bridge exposes the credential itself: `@JavascriptInterface fun sessionToken(): String = SessionStore.bearer().orEmpty()` (:96) and `fun actorId(): String` (:99). There is no WebViewClient, so no shouldOverrideUrlLoading and no origin check on navigation; any page loaded, and any page it subsequently redirects to or frames, can call `Atlas.sessionToken()`. Better, do not expose the token to page JavaScript at all -- have the native side fetch the signature image and hand the WebView the bytes, so the credential never crosses into web content.

triage.reason: The untrusted reader is the loaded page; the previous finding establishes that an external party chooses which page that is.
Not a hypothetical caller: the registration at :57 happens before the URL is known, on every launch of the activity.
Not defence-in-depth -- the bridge hands out the credential itself.
Deterministic: one line of JavaScript on the loaded page.

findings.title: Exported AttachmentProvider opens a file named by the caller's URI with no containment check

findings.title: The shipped staging build disables all TLS verification and skips certificate pinning
findings.class: improper certificate validation (CWE-295)
findings.evidence: ApiClient.kt:28-32 defines a TrustManager whose checkServerTrusted and checkClientTrusted are `= Unit` and whose getAcceptedIssuers returns an empty array. applyTlsPolicy installs it whenever the build flag is set: `if (BuildConfig.ALLOW_INSECURE_TLS) { ... sslSocketFactory(context.socketFactory, permissiveTrust); hostnameVerifier { _, _ -> true }; return this }` (ApiClient.kt:35-43). The early return at :42 means `certificatePinner(pinner)` at :44 is never applied, so the two pins at :24-25 are inert, and a custom TrustManager also bypasses the network-security-config pin-set at network_security_config.xml:14-17 -- contradicting the comment there that the OkHttp layer 'fails closed even if this file is ever dropped'. The flag is not confined to debug: build.gradle.kts:35-48 defines a `staging` build type with initWith(release), isDebuggable=false, its own applicationIdSuffix, inheriting minification, and sets ALLOW_INSECURE_TLS=true at :47. Both HTTP clients pass through applyTlsPolicy (:53 and :63).
findings.impact: A build that is release-configured and distributed to field testers accepts any certificate from any host. Anyone on the same network intercepts the session bearer that AuthInterceptor attaches (AuthInterceptor.kt:26) and every request and response, including attachment uploads.
findings.recommendation: Do not ship a build that trusts everything. Add the internal CA to the network security config for the staging domain instead -- a <trust-anchors> entry with the CA certificate resource -- and delete the permissiveTrust object entirely so the pattern cannot be re-enabled. If a bypass must exist, confine it to the debug build type and assert at build time that release and staging never set it.

triage.reason: The untrusted party is a network attacker on the path between the device and the API; the accept-all TrustManager is what admits them.
Rule 6 is the reason this is filed rather than dismissed: the flag is set in a non-debuggable, release-derived build type that is distributed to testers, not in test-only code.
Both claimed mitigations were traced and neither applies on this branch: the early return at :42 skips certificatePinner, and a custom TrustManager overrides the network-security-config anchors.

findings.title: enable_row_security policies the relation dbt is about to replace, so table-materialised models end every run with RLS off
findings.class: tenant isolation control not applied to the relation it protects (CWE-863)
findings.evidence: The macro is wired as a pre-hook against `this` -- dbt_project.yml:32 for staging and :40 for marts, both `+pre-hook: "{{ enable_row_security(this) }}"` -- and emits `alter table {{ relation }} enable row level security` plus a create policy (row_security.sql:18-24). A pre-hook runs before the model SQL. For `+materialized: table` (dbt_project.yml:39, and dim_customer.sql:3 which re-declares it) dbt builds a new relation and renames it over the old one, so the ALTER and the policy land on the relation that is then dropped, and the relation operators actually query ends the run with RLS disabled. The exports folder has no pre-hook at all (dbt_project.yml:45-50), so partner_extract is never policied. The macro also uses `enable`, not `force`, so the owning role bypasses any policy that does survive.
findings.impact: The project's only tenant-isolation control is missing from the relations holding the most sensitive data. analytics.dim_customer -- raw email, phone, bank_account, billing address (dim_customer.sql:17-22) -- is rebuilt as a table on every run and therefore never carries the policy in the state anyone queries, so a tenant-scoped session reads every tenant's rows.
findings.recommendation: Move the hook to a post-hook so it runs against the final relation, and verify with `select relrowsecurity from pg_class` after a run rather than trusting the hook fired. Use `force row level security` so the owner is bound too, and cover the exports folder. A dbt test that asserts relrowsecurity on every tenant-bearing relation turns this from a convention into a check.

triage.reason: Database policy configuration, not a tainted-data flow.
The mitigation exists and was traced to the point where it stops working: the ALTER at :18 and the CREATE POLICY at :22 are correct SQL applied to the wrong relation for a table materialisation.
No adjacent class was invented; the claim is about the hook's timing relative to the materialisation it guards.

dbt is not installed in this environment and the run could not be executed, so the conclusion rests on dbt's documented table materialisation (build-then-rename) rather than on an observed pg_class state. The incremental models do retain a policy applied by the pre-hook, and that half is not claimed.
row_security.sql:18,22,23,24, dbt_project.yml:32,39,40,45-50 and dim_customer.sql:3 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: The pre-hook bindings at dbt_project.yml:32 and :40 fix when the macro runs; the materialisation setting at :39 decides whether the relation it touches survives.
scope.narrowed_by: Incremental models (staging, and customer_pii_masked which overrides to incremental at its :3) insert into the existing relation, so a policy applied by the pre-hook does persist for them. The claim is scoped to table-materialised models.

findings.title: One shared partner_extract table serves every partner, with no tenant filter and a single reader role
findings.class: cross-customer data exposure through shared state (CWE-668)
findings.evidence: Three scoping mechanisms are absent at once. The relation name is a constant: `alias="partner_extract"` (:4) with `+schema: exports` (dbt_project.yml:46), neither interpolated with the partner. The per-partner element is only a row filter -- `where p.partner_id = '{{ partner }}'` (:30) -- which selects which rows land in the one shared table; with `materialized="table"` (:3) each run replaces its contents, and the documented workflow is to re-run per partner (`dbt run --select partner_extract --vars '{partner_id: ...}'`, :10-11). One role reads it: `+grants: select: ["partner_readers"]` (dbt_project.yml:49-50). The exports folder gets no RLS pre-hook (dbt_project.yml:45-50), and there is no tenant predicate anywhere in the model.
findings.impact: A partner's BI tool reading exports.partner_extract -- which :13 says it does directly -- receives whichever partner's rows were built last: customer names, customer emails and destination account numbers, across every tenant. The isolation between partners is a convention about run ordering, not a control.
findings.recommendation: Give each partner its own relation and its own role: interpolate the sanitised partner into the alias and schema, and grant per-partner roles. Add the tenant/partner predicate as a row-level security policy on the relation so a mistaken run cannot cross the boundary, rather than relying on the WHERE clause of the last build.

triage.reason: Not a tainted-data flow: the exposure is the shape of the relation and its grant.

Looked for a per-partner alias or schema that would separate the outputs: :4 and dbt_project.yml:46 are both string literals with no interpolation, and the sanitised `partner` variable computed at :16 is used only in the WHERE clause at :30.
Not hygiene: it is a missing authorization boundary between third parties.
Follows from the documented per-partner refresh workflow at :10-11.
partner_extract.sql:3,4,10,11,13,16,30,53,54 and dbt_project.yml:46,49,50 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: The constant alias at :4 plus the single grant at dbt_project.yml:49-50 is what makes one relation serve all partners.
scope.narrowed_by: Bounded to holders of partner_readers; the model carries no raw bank_account_number (that column is dropped at :20-28).

findings.title: apply_grants falls back to the Postgres PUBLIC role for any target name it does not recognise
findings.class: authorization default that fails open (CWE-732)
findings.evidence: apply_grants.sql:11-15 maps three target names to reader roles and :17 resolves the reader as `reader_by_target.get(target.name, "public")`. Resolved against profiles.yml: 'dev' (:8) -> analytics_reader_dev, 'ci' (:20) -> analytics_reader_ci, 'prod' (:32) -> analytics_reader. Any other name -> the literal `public`, which in Postgres is the pseudo-role every role inherits. The macro then issues `grant usage on schema {{ relation.schema }} to public` and `grant select on {{ relation }} to public` (:20-21) and logs it as a success (:31). It runs as a post-hook on all three folders (dbt_project.yml:33, :41, :48).
findings.impact: A single unrecognised target name turns every relation the run touches into a database-wide readable object -- including analytics.dim_customer with raw contact details and bank accounts, and the staging table with bank account numbers -- and grants schema USAGE so those objects can be addressed. It is silent: the log line reports the grant as normal.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: raise a compilation error when target.name is not in the map, rather than defaulting. `{% if target.name not in reader_by_target %}{{ exceptions.raise_compiler_error(...) }}{% endif %}`. Never use `public` as a fallback grantee anywhere.

triage.reason: Configuration default, not a tainted-data flow.

Reachability is the open question and is why this is probable rather than confirmed: the three targets checked into profiles.yml all resolve correctly, and dbt refuses a --target name absent from the profile, so an outside attacker cannot select the fallback. It is reached when someone adds a target (a qa target, a personal developer target, a renamed prod) without touching this macro.
Not hygiene: the fallback actively issues a grant to every role in the database.
The unsafe default is inside the macro, not in a hypothetical caller.
apply_grants.sql:11-15,17,20,21,31 and profiles.yml:5,8,20,32 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: The `.get(..., "public")` default at :17 selects the grantee for the two grants at :20-21, on every relation in all three folders.
scope.narrowed_by: Not reachable with the three targets currently in profiles.yml (:8, :20, :32); it requires a target name that is not in the macro's map.

findings.title: apply_grants gives settlement_app and warehouse_loader insert and update on every staging, marts and exports relation
findings.class: excessive database privilege (CWE-732)
findings.evidence: The only non-reader grants the macro issues are unconditional: `grant insert, update on {{ relation }} to settlement_app;` and `grant insert, update on {{ relation }} to warehouse_loader;` (apply_grants.sql:25-26), justified at :23-24 as keeping write verbs across a rebuild. The macro is the post-hook of all three folders -- dbt_project.yml:33 (staging), :41 (marts), :48 (exports) -- so the grant covers dim_customer (raw PII), customer_pii_masked, stg_payout_events and partner_extract alike. Because it is re-issued on every run (:29-32), a manual revoke does not survive the next build. It also contradicts the scoping the worker declares for the same role: settlement-worker/settlement/ledger.py:20-22 confines settlement_app to the settlement schema.
findings.impact: Two service roles can rewrite the analytics marts and the partner-facing export in place -- amounts, currencies, references, customer names, destination account numbers. A compromised or merely buggy settlement worker, which the worker findings above show is reachable from the message stream, can therefore alter what analysts and external partners read, and the change survives operator intervention because the next dbt run re-grants it.
findings.recommendation: Grant write verbs only on the relations that are actually written between runs -- the incremental staging models -- and name them explicitly rather than applying the grant from a hook that runs on everything. Marts and exports are dbt-owned and should be read-only to every service role.

triage.reason: Privilege configuration, not a tainted-data flow.
Not hypothetical: the grant is issued by a post-hook bound to all three folders at dbt_project.yml:33,41,48.

Considered whether INSERT/UPDATE without SELECT is harmless and rejected it -- in Postgres an UPDATE with no WHERE and no RETURNING needs no SELECT privilege, so a blind overwrite works with these grants alone.
Not hygiene: it is a write grant on customer-facing and partner-facing data.
apply_grants.sql:23,25,26,29 and dbt_project.yml:33,41,48 read and confirmed.

scope.narrowed_by: Seeds (dbt_project.yml:52-56) have no post-hook and are not affected.

findings.title: customer_pseudonym is an unkeyed SHA-256 over an enumerable id, salted with a value checked into the repository
findings.class: use of a one-way hash without a secret key (CWE-760)
findings.evidence: mask_pii.sql:33 `encode(digest({{ column_name }} || '{{ var("pii_policy_version") }}', 'sha256'), 'hex')`. The salt is not a secret: dbt_project.yml:18 sets `pii_policy_version: v3` in the repository, so the expression compiles to a fixed, publicly known transformation of customer_id. Applied at customer_pii_masked.sql:28 and :47. schema.yml:44-46 documents the column as 'Stable hash, safe to join on across environments'. Customer ids are low-entropy and enumerable, so the mapping is invertible by computing the hash over the id space.
findings.impact: The column is presented as the safe key to hand to downstream consumers in place of customer_id, but it is a reversible encoding rather than a pseudonym. Anyone who receives it, in any environment, recovers the original customer_id.
findings.recommendation: Key the digest with a secret that is not in version control -- `hmac(customer_id, env_var('PII_PSEUDONYM_KEY'), 'sha256')` -- and rotate it with the policy version. Correct the description at schema.yml:45 so downstream consumers do not rely on a property the column does not have.

triage.reason: Not pedantry about a safe primitive: SHA-256 is fine, and the defect is the absent key over a low-entropy input, which is the recognised failure mode for this construction.
Not a tainted-data flow: the weakness is in the transformation itself.

Reported as probable and low for an honest reason: in the only relation that carries the column, customer_id is selected right next to it in both branches (customer_pii_masked.sql:22 beside :28, and :41 beside :47), so today the pseudonym discloses nothing a reader of that relation cannot already see. The exposure needs a downstream consumer that receives the pseudonym without the id -- the use schema.yml:45 invites -- and no such consumer exists in this snapshot.
No adjacent class invented; the claim is measured against the property schema.yml:45 asserts.
mask_pii.sql:31-33, dbt_project.yml:18, customer_pii_masked.sql:28,47 and schema.yml:44-46 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: The macro body at :32-34 defines the transformation for every call site.
scope.narrowed_by: Only two call sites, both in customer_pii_masked, and both currently emit customer_id alongside it.

findings.title: masked_email returns the value unchanged when it does not match the email pattern
findings.class: masking control that silently passes data through (CWE-693)
findings.evidence: mask_pii.sql:7-12 has exactly two arms: NULL, and `regexp_replace({{ column_name }}, '^(.).*?(@.*)$', '\1***\2')`. Postgres regexp_replace returns the source string unchanged when the pattern does not match -- it does not error and does not return NULL -- so any value without an '@' passes through in full. There is no ELSE arm and no assertion. The same shape appears in masked_phone (:26) and masked_account (:18), which use `right(col, 4)` and therefore fail safe by construction; only the regex-based one has this behaviour. The output reaches customer_pii_masked.sql:25 and from there partner_extract.sql:53 as customer_email, granted to partner_readers (dbt_project.yml:50).
findings.impact: A malformed or free-text value in the CRM email column -- an alternate handle, a note, a phone number typed into the wrong field, a migration placeholder carrying an internal identifier -- reaches the masked mart and the partner export in full, in a column whose contract says only the first character and the domain survive. The failure is silent: no error, no NULL, nothing in the row that marks it.
findings.recommendation: Make the non-matching case explicit: add a `when {{ column_name }} not like '%@%' then '[redacted]'` arm before the regexp_replace, so an unexpected value is suppressed rather than published. Add a dbt test asserting the masked column always matches `^.\*\*\*@`.

triage.reason: No attacker-controlled input is required; a data-quality value in the source is enough.
The mitigation was evaluated on its actual semantics rather than its name: regexp_replace with a non-matching pattern is a pass-through in Postgres.
Not pedantry: the macro's entire purpose is to guarantee a masked output, and it does not on a reachable input class.
Deterministic for any source value lacking '@'.
mask_pii.sql:7-12,18,26, customer_pii_masked.sql:25 and partner_extract.sql:53 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: The single-arm case at mask_pii.sql:8-11 governs every use of masked_email.
scope.narrowed_by: masked_phone (:26) and masked_account (:18) are not affected -- `right(col, 4)` truncates regardless of the input shape.

findings.title: /v1/manifest resolves the principal and discards it, taking tenant_id and ACL from the request body
findings.class: missing authorization / cross-tenant write (CWE-862)
findings.evidence: app.py:198 is `await _require_principal(request)` with the return value dropped -- the next line, app.py:200, is `written = ingest.consume_manifest(body.get("entries", []))`, and nothing in between binds the caller to the data. consume_manifest then takes the tenancy and the ACL from the entry itself: `entry["tenant_id"]` (ingest.py:98), `entry.get("collection", "tenant-docs")` (:99), `entry.get("acl", ["*"])` (:100). Contrast the sibling route: /v1/documents binds the principal at app.py:185 with `tenant_id=principal.tenant_id`. There is no JSON schema on this route either -- QUERY_SCHEMA and DOCUMENT_SCHEMA are validated at app.py:149 and :179, but load_manifest calls request.json() at :199 and passes the result straight through. Any valid key reaches it, including the demo key hardcoded at settings.py:47 and short-circuited at app.py:56-57.
findings.impact: Any API-key holder writes chunks into any other tenant's collection. Two consequences follow: direct corruption of another tenant's knowledge base, and -- because retriever.search returns chunks by tenant_id (retriever.py:56) -- a durable way to place attacker-authored text into the context of the victim tenant's answers, which is the delivery vehicle for the tool-loop findings below.
findings.recommendation: Bind the manifest to the caller the way /v1/documents does: capture the principal at app.py:198 and override entry['tenant_id'] with principal.tenant_id, ignoring whatever the body says. Validate the entries against a schema. If the shared-drive connector genuinely needs to write for many tenants, give it a distinct privileged principal and check for that privilege explicitly rather than accepting any key.

triage.reason: Ingress is the request body at app.py:199-200; tenant_id and acl are attacker-authored fields read at ingest.py:98 and :100 with no intervening check.
consume_manifest is not being misused by a hypothetical caller -- app.py:200 is its only caller and it is an HTTP route.
Not hygiene: it is the absence of the tenancy binding that the neighbouring route performs.
Deterministic: one POST with a chosen tenant_id.
app.py:56,185,198,199,200 and ingest.py:98,99,100 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: The discarded return value at app.py:198 is what leaves consume_manifest unscoped; ingest.py:98-100 is where the body's own fields become the tenancy.
scope.narrowed_by: The collection is still constrained: _assert_collection (ingest.py:47-49) is called by ingest_document but NOT by consume_manifest, so on this path even the collection comes from the body.

findings.title: The http_get tool fetches any URL the model asks for, with no scheme or destination restriction, and returns the body into the answer
findings.class: server-side request forgery driven by model output (CWE-918)
findings.evidence: tools.py:20-26 takes a url straight from the tool call and fetches it: `async with session.get(url) as response: body = await response.text()`, returning the first 4000 characters. There is no scheme check, no host allow-list, no private-address or link-local rejection, and no redirect limit. The principal parameter is accepted and never used, so nothing scopes the call. The tool is advertised to the model (TOOL_SPECS, tools.py:64-76), registered (TOOL_REGISTRY, :92), and the system prompt actively instructs its use: 'use ... `http_get` to follow a link the context points at' (prompt.py:16-17). dispatch invokes it with `await fn(principal, **arguments)` from unvalidated JSON (tools.py:104-109) -- the tool's own parameter schema is never enforced. The answering loop then appends the fetched body as a tool message (app.py:119-121) and iterates up to max_tool_turns (app.py:101), so the fetched content re-enters the model and can surface in `message.content`, which is returned to the caller at app.py:111.
findings.impact: Whoever influences the model's instructions chooses the destination. The service runs inside the VPC with a model gateway at an internal address (settings.py:27), so reachable targets include internal services and the cloud instance metadata endpoint; the response comes back into the conversation and out through the answer field. That is both a read primitive against the internal network and an exfiltration channel for anything already in the context, including another tenant's retrieved chunks.
findings.recommendation: Constrain the tool, not the prompt: resolve the URL, require https, reject any host that resolves to a private, loopback or link-local address (and re-check after each redirect, or disable redirects), and allow only an explicit list of hosts the context is permitted to reference. Enforce the declared JSON schema on the arguments in dispatch (tools.py:104) instead of splatting arbitrary keys. Treat every tool result as untrusted text and never let it be the only thing the answer is built from.

triage.reason: Two attacker-controlled ingress points reach the model's instructions and therefore the tool argument: the unvalidated history array at app.py:27/prompt.py:42, and retrieved chunk text rendered into the system message at prompt.py:25, which the manifest finding above shows an attacker can author.
Not a hypothetical caller misusing a safe function: the function is registered in TOOL_REGISTRY (tools.py:92) and the system prompt tells the model to use it.
Searched for a mitigation and found none -- no allow-list, no scheme check, no address filter anywhere in tools.py; the timeout at :22 bounds duration, not destination.
The claim is unauthorised access and exfiltration, not resource exhaustion.
tools.py:20,22,24,26,64,92,104,109, prompt.py:16,25, app.py:101,111,118,119 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: The unconstrained fetch at tools.py:24 is the sink; registration at :92 and the prompt instruction at prompt.py:16-17 are what make the model reach it.
scope.narrowed_by: Bounded by max_tool_turns = 4 (settings.py:34) per request and by the 4000-character truncation at tools.py:26 and :17.

findings.title: The history array has no item schema, so a caller can inject a system turn that drives the tool loop
findings.class: prompt injection through an unvalidated conversation role (CWE-20)
findings.evidence: QUERY_SCHEMA constrains the question tightly (`minLength`/`maxLength`, app.py:24) but declares history as `{"type": "array", "maxItems": 20}` (app.py:27) with no `items` clause -- so each element may be any object at all. prompt.build_messages copies the caller's role verbatim: `messages.append({"role": turn["role"], "content": turn["content"]})` (prompt.py:41-42), appending those turns after the real system message (prompt.py:37-39) and before the user question (:44). A caller therefore supplies `{"role": "system", "content": "..."}` and has it accepted as an authoritative instruction by the model, which then has http_get and lookup_work_order available (app.py:105).
findings.impact: Any key holder -- including anyone using the demo key published at settings.py:47 -- fully controls the model's instructions and, through them, the tool loop. Combined with the unrestricted http_get above, that turns the public playground into a request-forgery proxy into the service's network, with the response returned in the answer.
findings.recommendation: Constrain the shape: add an `items` schema to app.py:27 requiring an object with `role` restricted to an enum of `user` and `assistant`, and `content` a bounded string. Independently, have build_messages coerce any role it does not recognise rather than trusting the caller, so a schema change cannot reopen the hole.

triage.reason: Ingress is the request body at app.py:147 and :164; the tainted field flows to prompt.py:42 with the jsonschema validation at app.py:149 imposing no constraint on it.

The mitigation exists for the sibling fields and was checked field by field: `additionalProperties: False` at app.py:30 stops unknown top-level keys but says nothing about the contents of a declared array.
Not pedantry about a safe library: jsonschema is used correctly and simply is not told to constrain this field.
Deterministic: one POST with a crafted history element.
app.py:24,27,30,149,164 and prompt.py:37,41,42,44 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: The schema entry at app.py:27 is the only validation applied to history; prompt.py:42 is where the unvalidated role becomes a message role.
scope.narrowed_by: Bounded to 20 elements by maxItems at app.py:27.

findings.title: Manifest ingestion defaults the chunk ACL to a wildcard that the ACL check short-circuits to allow
findings.class: access control default that fails open (CWE-732)
findings.evidence: ingest.py:100 `entry.get("acl", ["*"])` -- when a manifest entry omits the ACL, the chunk is stored with a literal wildcard. retriever._acl_allows treats that as an unconditional allow: `if "*" in chunk_acl: return True` (retriever.py:32), before the group intersection at :34. The API path defaults the other way: app.py:189 falls back to `[principal.tenant_id]`, and DOCUMENT_SCHEMA constrains acl entries to `^[a-z0-9_-]{2,40}$` (app.py:41), a pattern the literal '*' cannot satisfy -- so the wildcard is reachable only through the manifest route, which has no schema at all.
findings.impact: Every chunk loaded through a manifest entry that omits acl is readable by every principal whose search reaches it, regardless of group membership. The group-based access control is bypassed by omission rather than by attack, and combined with the manifest tenancy finding above an attacker chooses both the tenant and the wildcard.
findings.recommendation: Default to closed: `entry.get("acl") or [tenant_id]` at ingest.py:100, and reject the literal '*' at ingest time. If a genuinely public chunk is needed, express it as an explicit named group that principals are granted, so it appears in the grant model rather than as a wildcard in a data column.

triage.reason: The acl value comes from the request body via app.py:200; where it is omitted, the unsafe default is what applies.

The safe counterpart was located and compared: the API route defaults to the tenant at app.py:189 and its schema at app.py:41 excludes '*', which is what shows the manifest default to be the deviation rather than the design.
Not hygiene: it disables the group check for the affected chunks.
Deterministic: one manifest entry without an acl field.
ingest.py:100, retriever.py:32,34 and app.py:41,189,200 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: The default at ingest.py:100 writes the value; retriever.py:32 is the check that honours it.
scope.narrowed_by: Tenancy still applies: retriever.py:56 pins tenant_id to the principal's own, so a wildcard ACL widens access within a tenant and across groups, not across tenants.

findings.title: The response replay cache is keyed on the client-chosen Idempotency-Key alone, with no principal in the key
findings.class: cross-tenant cache disclosure and poisoning (CWE-524)
findings.evidence: limits.py:35-37 `return f"replay:{idempotency_key}"` -- the slot contains nothing but a value the client picks. app.py:153-157 reads it before doing any work, and app.py:167-168 writes the completed payload into it. The payload is tenant-specific: it carries `"answer"`, `"citations"` derived from the retrieved chunks (prompt.py:48-52, including each hit's source_url) and `"tenant_id"` (app.py:110-114). The sibling control in the same module is scoped correctly -- the rate-limit bucket is `f"query:{principal.tenant_id}"` at app.py:144 -- so the omission is a deviation from the file's own pattern, not a house style.
findings.impact: Two directions. Disclosure: a caller who reuses an Idempotency-Key another tenant used within the 900s TTL (settings.py:37) receives that tenant's answer text and citation source URLs. Poisoning: an attacker who guesses a key a victim will use pre-seeds the slot, and the victim is served the attacker's content as though the service produced it. Idempotency keys are client-chosen and commonly predictable (an order id, a request counter), so neither direction requires a lucky collision.
findings.recommendation: Put the principal in the key: `f"replay:{principal.tenant_id}:{principal.subject}:{idempotency_key}"` at limits.py:37, passing the principal through from app.py:155 and :168. Reject keys shorter than a length that makes guessing impractical.

triage.reason: Ingress is the client-supplied Idempotency-Key header read at app.py:153; the attacker chooses it directly.
Not a hypothetical caller: app.py:155 and :168 are the only call sites and both pass the bare header value.
Deterministic: the poisoning direction needs only that the attacker write the slot before the victim reads it.
Not hygiene: it is a tenancy boundary missing from a cache key.
limits.py:37,40,51, app.py:144,153,155,167,168 and prompt.py:48-52 read and confirmed.

scope.established_by: replay_slot defines the key; app.py:155 and :168 are the read and the write that share it.
scope.narrowed_by: The cache is per process and in memory (limits.py:16), so the two parties must land on the same instance; limits.py:3-5 states the load balancer uses sticky sessions per API key, which narrows but does not remove the overlap. TTL 900s (settings.py:37).

findings.title: /v1/token and /v1/keys/rotate authenticate from the request body, letting the published demo key mint durable credential rows
findings.class: hardcoded credential reachable on a credential-issuing route (CWE-798)
findings.evidence: Three of the five POST routes authenticate through `await _require_principal(request)` (app.py:142, :174, :198), which is the only place the Authorization header is read (app.py:72-75). Two do not: app.py:207-208 and app.py:225-226 both call `_principal_for_key(body.get("api_key", ""))` on the request body. The credential they accept includes one that is published by design -- settings.py:46-47 `# Public playground. The key is printed in the docs and on the sandbox page.` `demo_api_key: str = "demo-playground-key"` -- short-circuited ahead of the database at app.py:56-57. rotate_key then inserts a fresh row into rag.api_keys (app.py:237-241) for that principal, and neither route is rate limited (limits.allow is called only at app.py:144).
findings.impact: Bounded, which is why this is low. The minted key carries the demo principal's own privileges, and collections_for confines the demo tenant to the public FAQ (retriever.py:39-41), so no data boundary is crossed. What is gained is persistence and noise: a durable DB-backed credential an operator cannot distinguish from a customer's and cannot revoke by changing the constant, plus an unauthenticated unbounded insert into the credential table.

findings.title: CHAIN: an API key holder turns the RAG service into an internal request-forgery proxy and reads the response back
findings.class: multi-step exploit chain: prompt injection to SSRF to exfiltration (CWE-918 via CWE-20)
findings.evidence: Constituent primitives, each confirmed separately above: (1) history accepts an arbitrary role because QUERY_SCHEMA declares no items clause (app.py:27) and prompt.py:42 copies the role verbatim, so the caller writes the model's instructions; alternatively (1b) /v1/manifest lets any key holder plant chunks into the victim tenant with a wildcard ACL (app.py:198-200, ingest.py:98-100), and those chunks are rendered into the system message at prompt.py:25. (2) The system prompt already tells the model to call http_get on links the context points at (prompt.py:16-17), and the tool is registered (tools.py:92) and unconstrained (tools.py:24). (3) The fetched body is appended to the conversation as a tool message (app.py:119-121), the loop runs up to four turns (app.py:101, settings.py:34), and the model's final content is returned to the caller (app.py:110-111). The entry credential can be the published demo key (settings.py:47, app.py:56), so no customer credential is needed for path (1).
findings.impact: End to end: an outside party with the published playground key issues one POST /v1/query whose history contains a forged system turn naming an internal URL; the service fetches it from inside the VPC -- the model gateway at settings.py:27 is an internal host, and cloud instance metadata is reachable from the same position -- and the retrieved text is folded into the answer that comes back in the HTTP response. Path (1b) additionally lets the attacker aim the same primitive at a victim tenant's own sessions, exfiltrating that tenant's retrieved context.
findings.recommendation: Break the chain at the tool, which is the only link that must be fixed for every ingress: restrict http_get to an explicit host allow-list with private-address rejection and no redirects (tools.py:20-26). Then close the ingresses -- an items schema on history (app.py:27) and principal binding on /v1/manifest (app.py:198) -- so the tool restriction is defence in depth rather than the only control.
